column1: Where does control go when a catchable error occurs inside TRY?
column2: To the associated CATCH block.
column3: The remaining statements in that TRY block are skipped.

column1: Where does control go after TRY finishes without an error?
column2: To the statement after END CATCH.
column3: The associated CATCH block is skipped.

column1: Where does execution normally resume when CATCH finishes without rethrowing or returning?
column2: After END CATCH.
column3: It does not resume at the failed statement inside TRY.

column1: Why rethrow an unexpected caught error after cleanup?
column2: The caller does not receive the caught exception automatically.
column3: A CATCH block that only logs an error can hide the failure from its caller.

column1: Which compilation errors bypass TRY...CATCH at the same execution level?
column2: Errors such as syntax errors that prevent the batch from running.
column3: The same-level handler cannot run when its batch cannot compile.

column1: How can an outer TRY catch a missing-table error from dynamic SQL?
column2: Execute that statement through sp_executesql inside TRY.
column3: Object resolution then occurs at a lower execution level.

column1: What happens to local CATCH handling if an error closes the database connection?
column2: It cannot run in that terminated connection.
column3: Some severity-20-or-higher errors remain catchable if the connection survives.

column1: How does TRY...CATCH treat a severity-10 informational message?
column2: It does not transfer control to CATCH.
column3: Messages with severity 10 or lower are outside its catchable error range.

column1: Why does ERROR_MESSAGE remain reliable after other successful statements in the same CATCH?
column2: Its value is scoped to the caught error.
column3: Successful statements and repeated reads do not consume that error information.

column1: What does ERROR_PROCEDURE return for a caught error raised outside any stored procedure or trigger?
column2: NULL.
column3: An ad hoc batch error can still have an error number and message.

column1: In a nested CATCH, which error does ERROR_MESSAGE describe?
column2: The error that invoked that CATCH.
column3: The outer CATCH keeps its own error context.

column1: What happens to the original error number when CATCH uses bare THROW;?
column2: It is preserved.
column3: Creating a new numbered exception replaces that number.

column1: Why must logging precede bare THROW in a CATCH?
column2: THROW transfers control, so later logging statements do not run.
column3: Log the details before propagating the failure to the caller.

column1: What can THROW's state distinguish when the same error number is raised at several locations?
column2: The location that raised the error.
column3: Assign distinct states to different raise sites.

column1: Which function can prepare a formatted message for THROW?
column2: FORMATMESSAGE.
column3: Assign its result to a message variable before passing that variable to THROW.

column1: Why must code using RAISERROR handle transaction rollback explicitly?
column2: RAISERROR does not honor SET XACT_ABORT.
column3: An error message alone is not transaction cleanup.

column1: What groups several data changes into an all-or-nothing operation?
column2: An explicit transaction with appropriate commit and rollback handling.
column3: TRY...CATCH alone does not make several statements atomic.

column1: For a procedure-owned all-or-nothing transaction, when does the success path commit?
column2: After all required operations succeed.
column3: Keep the commit on the successful TRY path.

column1: Why does @@TRANCOUNT > 0 not prove that COMMIT is allowed?
column2: It reports transaction count, not committability.
column3: Use XACT_STATE() to check whether the transaction can be committed.

column1: Why must CATCH still check transaction state with XACT_ABORT ON?
column2: A caught error can leave an active transaction that cannot be committed.
column3: Automatic abort does not guarantee rollback before CATCH executes.

column1: Which error phase is not covered by XACT_ABORT?
column2: Compilation, including syntax errors.
column3: XACT_ABORT is a run-time error option.

column1: With XACT_ABORT OFF, what can happen after a statement-level runtime error?
column2: Only the failed statement rolls back, leaving the transaction active.
column3: Other errors can still abort the entire transaction.

column1: Why check for an active transaction before ROLLBACK in CATCH?
column2: Some errors already roll back the transaction.
column3: Rolling back with no active transaction causes another error.

column1: What rollback is permitted when XACT_STATE() = -1?
column2: A full transaction rollback, not a savepoint rollback.
column3: The transaction cannot perform writes or commit.

column1: For a procedure-owned uncommittable transaction, when can CATCH insert into a normal ErrorLog table?
column2: After fully rolling back the failed transaction.
column3: An uncommittable transaction rejects ordinary table writes, including logging.

column1: When only the outer procedure starts a shared transaction, which procedure coordinates rollback in the unit's pattern?
column2: The outer procedure.
column3: The inner procedure rethrows so the owning outer CATCH can clean up.

column1: If @@TRANCOUNT is 2, what does ROLLBACK TRANSACTION without a savepoint do?
column2: Rolls back the full transaction and sets @@TRANCOUNT to 0.
column3: Nested BEGIN TRANSACTION calls do not create independently rolled-back transactions.

column1: How can CATCH handle catchable errors from its own logging code?
column2: Use a nested TRY...CATCH around the logging operation.
column3: An error does not re-enter the CATCH block already running.

column1: Why is XACT_STATE() = 1 insufficient reason to commit an all-or-nothing operation after an error?
column2: Committable does not mean every required operation succeeded.
column3: Roll back incomplete work even when the transaction can still be committed.
